reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: A circadian rhythm disorder in which the internal clock fails to entrain to the 24-hour day, so sleep and wake times drift progressively later
The sleep period cycles in and out of alignment with the desired schedule, giving alternating good and bad periods
It is most common in totally blind people, who lack the light input needed to entrain the clock
In sighted individuals it is rare and may relate to reduced light sensitivity, behavioural factors or an underlying delayed sleep phase
A prolonged sleep diary or actigraphy demonstrating the steadily drifting sleep pattern is central to diagnosis
Appropriately timed melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist can entrain the rhythm, particularly in blind patients
In sighted patients, timed bright-light exposure combined with melatonin is used to reinforce entrainment
reference.pathophysiology: The suprachiasmatic nucleus generates an intrinsic rhythm that is on average slightly longer than 24 hours and is normally reset each day, mainly by light reaching the retina. When this entraining signal is absent, as in total blindness, or is ineffective, the clock runs free at its own period and sleep-wake timing drifts later day by day. Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland under circadian control, provides a complementary timing signal that can be supplied exogenously to help re-entrain the rhythm.
additionalInvestigations: Sleep diary maintained over several weeks to reveal the progressively drifting pattern
Actigraphy over an extended period to document the free-running sleep-wake timing
Assessment of visual function and light perception
Circadian phase markers such as dim-light melatonin onset where available
Review of medication, substance use and daytime light exposure
redFlags: New circadian disruption with neurological or cognitive decline suggesting a central cause
Severe daytime impairment with occupational or safety risk
Coexisting untreated mood disorder or suicidal ideation
Features suggesting a structural hypothalamic or pineal lesion
reference.prognosis: With correctly timed melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist, and light therapy in sighted patients, many achieve entrainment and stable sleep, though relapse is common if treatment timing lapses, and management is a long-term commitment.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the drifting pattern as simple insomnia and prescribing hypnotics
Giving melatonin at the wrong circadian time, which can fail to entrain or even worsen misalignment
Not recognising total blindness as the key predisposing factor
Overlooking the need for sustained, correctly timed treatment
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Entrain the circadian clock with correctly timed exogenous melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist such as tasimelteon, which is particularly effective in totally blind patients
Add timed morning bright-light therapy in sighted patients to strengthen photic entrainment
Reinforce a fixed sleep-wake schedule, good sleep hygiene, and regular social and activity time cues
Track response with an ongoing sleep diary and actigraphy to confirm entrainment and fine-tune the timing of treatment
Identify and treat associated mood disturbance arising from chronic circadian misalignment
Maintain treatment as a long-term commitment, since relapse is common when the timing of melatonin lapses
Refer to a sleep medicine specialist for circadian phase assessment and to guide dosing timing relative to circadian markers
